## The assembly meeting

You've called this meeting for one reason: finish the thing. Your systems administrator has
the eQMS's (electronic quality-management system's) CMDB (configuration management database)
entry open on one screen — every field filled in except the last one, still blank three modules
later. Your Quality Analyst (QA) has the service-catalog entry and the quality-system scope
statement open side by side on another, the same two documents that have quietly disagreed with
each other since you first drafted them.

"We've been pointing at these two gaps for weeks," your QA says. "Every module finds them again
and explains why they matter. At some point we have to actually fix them, not just understand
them better."

She's right, and today's the day. Nothing in this room is new work. The qualification field's
answer already exists — it's sitting in a different file, under a different name, and you proved
that yourself two modules ago. The Fairview mismatch has one honest resolution available right
now and a second one that needs a real decision, not a shrug. Your job this meeting isn't
discovery. It's assembly: take everything this course has already built and turn it into one
artifact that actually holds up when someone outside this room reads it cold.

## Why this matters — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure a half-assembled artifact produces, stated plainly before any framework
enters the room: **three different reviewers — an FDA investigator, an AABB assessor, a security
assessor — each ask a version of the same question ("is this system actually under control?"),
and Lakeshore answers it three different ways, in three different documents, because nobody ever
sat down and made them agree.** That's not a crisis by itself, any more than the blank field or
the Fairview mismatch was a crisis on its own. It's a slow, compounding liability: every reviewer
who finds a gap your own records could have closed is a reviewer who now has a reason to ask what
else hasn't been reconciled.

You already own the ITSM (IT service management) concept that names exactly this discipline,
even if you've never had to apply it under three sets of eyes at once: a **single source of
truth**. A CMDB's whole reason for existing, in plain ITIL practice, is that nobody should have to
guess which of five spreadsheets is the real one — there's one record, kept current, that
everyone defers to. A service catalog exists for the same reason, one layer up: one place that
says what IT actually offers, so a requester doesn't have to triangulate between an old email
and somebody's memory. You've run this discipline for years, for version numbers and dependency
maps. This module asks you to run the exact same discipline somewhere higher-stakes: one record
that an FDA investigator, an AABB assessor, and a security assessor can all read and all trust,
instead of three separately-maintained stories that happen to describe the same system.

## A note on citations: still none new here

This module introduces no new regulatory source, control number, or standard — the discipline
this entire course has held since module 1. Everything below reassembles facts this curriculum
already locked: `categorize-and-select-controls` and `authorize-and-monitor` (both
`grc-frameworks-and-risk-management`) hold the eQMS's full RMF (Risk Management Framework) file,
referenced here, not re-quoted — read those two modules for the actual citation decoder and
verbatim NIST text, the same pattern modules 1-3 of this course already set for a synthesis
module with nothing new to cite. `the-aabb-assessment-process`, `fda-inspection-authority-and-
outcomes`, and `warning-letters-and-recalls` (all `fda-and-aabb-in-practice`) are referenced by
name for what each reviewer actually checks, not redeveloped. `reading-a-soc-2-report` and
`reading-an-iso-27001-certificate` (both `vendor-and-third-party-risk-management`) are referenced
the same way for the security assessor's lens. No AABB Standard number, no ISO 27001 Annex A
control number, and no new ITIL publication citation appears anywhere below.

## Filling the blank: the CMDB's qualification field

Your systems administrator has his cursor sitting in the one field that's been blank since
module 2. "I keep wanting to write something here," he says. "A status. A date. Something.
But every time I start, it feels like I'd be making it up — we never ran a separate qualification
exercise for the eQMS the way BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) got one."

"You don't need a new exercise," your QA says. "You need a pointer. We already did this — it's
just sitting under RMF's name instead of a CMDB's."

That's the whole fix, and it's worth being precise about why it's not a shortcut. The field was
never asking "did someone run IQ/OQ/PQ (installation, operational, and performance qualification)
on this system" — it was asking "has anyone established, with evidence, whether this system is
fit to do the job it's doing." `categorize-and-select-controls` already answered that question in
full, with more rigor than a bare CMDB template would ever have demanded: the eQMS categorized as
**moderate-impact**, reasoned through three specific failure modes (CAPA-record alteration,
cross-site exposure, audit-log unavailability during an assessment), with three control families
sized to that finding. `authorize-and-monitor` already answered the follow-up question — is
anyone still checking — with a standing monitoring plan tied to a real authorization decision.

Here's the exact text going into the CMDB's qualification/validation-status field:

> **Categorized moderate-impact per RMF** (reasoned through three CIA — confidentiality,
> integrity, availability — failure modes specific to this system). **Three control families
> selected and implemented**: account and identity management, audit/logging, and physical and
> environmental protection. **Two confirmed operating as intended** at Assess (audit/logging;
> physical and environmental protection). **One — the quarterly access-review control, within
> account and identity management — accepted as a named, time-bound residual risk** at Authorize,
> not a failure: implemented and documented, its first scheduled cycle tracked under a 30-day
> remediation window, now folded into a standing monitoring plan (ongoing quarterly cadence,
> periodic audit-log spot-checks, a standing trigger to reopen the authorization on material
> change). Authorization: active. **Full file: `categorize-and-select-controls` and
> `authorize-and-monitor`.**

Read that against what the field looked like three modules ago: a note that it "wasn't a standard
CMDB field," blank by default. The difference isn't new work — it's the first time anyone wrote
the cross-reference down where a reader of the CMDB entry alone would actually find it. That's the
real teaching point, worth saying to your CIO (chief information officer) in one sentence: **a
gap in one record doesn't always need new work to close it. Sometimes it needs the two people who
each did real work, in two different systems, to finally read each other's files.**

## Reconciling Fairview: a correction, plus a dated decision

The second gap is messier, because unlike the qualification field, it isn't a missing
cross-reference — it's two documents making genuinely different claims about the same fact. Your
QA reads both versions out loud, the way she did the day she first caught it.

**The service catalog, drafted by IT, says:** document control is offered at the central site,
Brookfield, *and* Fairview.

**The scope statement, owned by Quality, says:** document control is in scope for the central
site and Brookfield only. Fairview's document-control records remain on paper, under the site's
existing process, pending migration.

"One of these is just wrong," your systems administrator says. "Let's fix the catalog and move
on." That's half right, and today it's exactly what happens — the catalog's wording changes to
stop claiming something that isn't true. But stopping there would just be a quieter version of
the same problem: the catalog would go from *actively false* to *silently accurate*, with the
real question — is Fairview's migration to the eQMS actually planned, and when — still sitting
unanswered, the way it's sat unanswered since module 2.

So the meeting does both things. First, the correction:

**The reconciled service-catalog entry:**

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| **Service** | eQMS |
| **Provides** | CAPA tracking (all three sites); internal-audit logging (all three sites); document control (central site and Brookfield — see note) |
| **Offered to** | Quality staff and site operations leadership |
| **Offered at** | Central site, Brookfield, and Fairview (full eQMS access for CAPA tracking and audit logging at all three; document-control access follows the note below) |
| **Service level** | Business-hours support; next-business-day response for access issues |
| **Note** | Fairview's document control remains on the site's existing paper-based process. This is not an unexplained mismatch — see the dated action item below. |

That brings the catalog into exact agreement with the scope statement your QA already owns —
no more "all three sites" claim for a service that only two sites actually receive. Second, the
part a silent correction would have skipped: your QA picks up her phone and calls Fairview's site
operations lead, the same conversation she should have had the day she first found the gap.
Fairview's paper-based process isn't frozen in place by accident — a migration has been informally
discussed for a while, with no committed date, because nobody ever made it anyone's actual job to
commit to one.

That changes today. The three of you agree on a real action item, not a vague intention:

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| **Action** | Migrate Fairview's document control onto the eQMS, matching central site and Brookfield |
| **Owner** | Systems administrator, with sign-off from the QA and Fairview's site operations lead |
| **Target** | Within two quarters |
| **Trigger to revisit if missed** | Raised at the next quarterly IT service review, the same standing cadence the continual-improvement register already uses |

Notice what this is and isn't. It isn't a new regulatory requirement — nothing in AABB's
framework or FDA regulation tells Lakeshore it must run document control electronically at every
site; a paper-based process, properly controlled, is a legitimate choice `quality-system-
essentials`'s own document-control module never ruled out. What changes is that "pending
migration" now has an owner and a date instead of sitting as a phrase in a scope statement nobody
had committed to acting on. A reviewer reading either document today finds the same honest story
twice: here's what's true right now, and here's exactly who's accountable for when it changes.

## Testing the artifact: three reviewers, one document

Here's the actual point of this module. You now have one CMDB entry and one service-catalog
entry, reconciled with each other and with the scope statement. Walk it past three different
readers, one at a time, the way this course's plan always intended this module to close.

**An FDA investigator** (reference `fda-inspection-authority-and-outcomes` and `warning-letters-
and-recalls`, don't redevelop). An investigator reviewing a system that holds CAPA records,
document control, and audit logs isn't grading your ITSM maturity — she's checking whether
Lakeshore's own records are internally consistent and whether the system producing them is under
control. Two things she'd ask for, and the reconciled artifact answers both: *is this system
qualified to produce reliable records?* — yes, with a direct pointer to the RMF file, not a blank
field or a vague assurance. *Do your own documents agree with each other about what this system
does and where?* — yes, now that the catalog and scope statement say the same thing, and the one
place they used to differ is itself documented as a tracked, dated action rather than something
she'd have to catch herself. `warning-letters-and-recalls` already named an unreconciled
documentation inconsistency as exactly the kind of finding that turns into a 483 observation; this
artifact is built specifically so that finding doesn't exist anymore.

**An AABB assessor** (reference `the-aabb-assessment-process`, don't redevelop). An assessor
running a QSE-based review checks something subtly different: not just whether the records agree,
but whether Lakeshore *found its own gaps before she did.* `the-aabb-assessment-process` already
teaches that a self-identified, actively-managed gap grades very differently than the same gap
discovered cold by the assessor. The Fairview line is the clean test case here — it's not hidden,
it's not glossed over, and it's not pretended-solved. It's named, dated, and owned. That's close
to the best outcome an organization can show on an open item: not zero gaps, but demonstrated
control over the gaps that exist.

**A security assessor** (reference `vendor-and-third-party-risk-management`'s `reading-a-soc-2-
report` and `reading-an-iso-27001-certificate`, don't redevelop). This is the reviewer worth being
most honest about, because the artifact does *not* fully satisfy her the way it satisfies the
other two. She'd find real, usable material: a complete CI record with identity, dependencies,
and ownership; a qualification field that traces cleanly to a documented RMF categorization and
control selection; a monitoring plan with named owners and real triggers. All of that reads like
good evidence toward an access-control domain, the one clean match `itil-to-grc-crosswalk` already
found between the eQMS's RMF work and ISO 27001's Annex A structure. But that same module was
honest about two domains with no counterpart at all in the eQMS's existing controls — supplier
relationships and business continuity — and nothing built in this assembly meeting changes that.
A security assessor running a real ISO 27001 or SOC 2-style review would still ask questions this
single artifact can't answer: what's Lakeshore's documented approach to the vendors behind the
eQMS's own infrastructure, and what's the tested plan if the eQMS itself goes down for an extended
period? Those aren't failures of this module's work — they're domains Lakeshore's RMF selection
was never asked to cover, named honestly back in module 3, and naming them again here instead of
quietly letting this artifact imply full coverage is the honest thing to do.

So the real answer to this course's own central question — does one artifact replace three
separate documents maintained in parallel? — is **mostly yes, with one named boundary**. For
"is this system under control, and do your own records agree with each other," one reconciled
CMDB-and-catalog entry genuinely satisfies an FDA investigator and an AABB assessor without any
separate document built just for them. For "does this system meet a full ISMS-grade security
review," the same artifact is strong partial evidence, not a complete answer — and saying so
plainly is worth more than a confident claim that wouldn't survive a specific follow-up question.

## Common traps

**"Filling in the qualification field means we need to go run a validation exercise on the
eQMS."** No — and treating it that way would waste real effort on work already done. The field
needed a pointer to rigor that already exists, not a new instance of that rigor. Confusing "this
field is blank" with "this work was never done" is the exact mistake this module exists to
correct.

**"Correcting the service-catalog wording is the whole fix."** It's half of it. A quietly
accurate document is better than an actively false one, but it leaves the real underlying
question — is Fairview's migration actually happening, and when — exactly as unanswered as it was
before. An artifact that looks reconciled but still has a live, undated "pending" sitting inside
it hasn't actually closed the gap; it's just made the gap harder to notice.

## What this means for your job

- **Before accepting any blank or inconsistent field in a quality-relevant system record as
  unsolved, ask whether the real answer already exists somewhere else under a different name.**
  That's the move that closed the qualification field here, and it generalizes to almost any
  cross-functional gap you'll find between IT's records and Quality's.
- **When you correct a stale or inaccurate catalog entry, don't stop at the correction.** Ask what
  real decision the inaccuracy was covering for, and give that decision an owner and a date, the
  way the Fairview migration got one in this meeting.
- **Know, for any artifact you're about to hand a reviewer, which of the three lenses it was
  actually built to satisfy — and say so plainly where it falls short**, instead of letting an
  investigator, assessor, or security auditor discover the boundary themselves. A named gap reads
  as control. A gap they find first reads as the opposite.
- **Treat "one source of truth" as a standard that applies above the CMDB, not just inside it.**
  The same discipline that keeps a CI record from drifting across teams is the discipline that
  keeps a service catalog and a scope statement from quietly disagreeing for months.
- **When you brief your CIO or your exec quality council on this artifact, lead with what it
  actually closes (the qualification pointer, the Fairview reconciliation) and name what it
  doesn't (a full ISO 27001-grade security picture)** — the same honest balance this course has
  held since its first crosswalk.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator asks whether filling in the CMDB's qualification field required running any new testing or validation work on the eQMS. Did it?

No. The field's answer already existed, in full, in `categorize-and-select-controls` and
`authorize-and-monitor` — the eQMS's moderate-impact categorization, its three control families,
and its standing monitoring plan. What changed in this module is that the CMDB entry now points
directly to that file instead of sitting blank. No new qualification exercise was run, and none
was needed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Does AABB or FDA require Lakeshore to migrate Fairview's document control onto the eQMS, the way the dated action item in this module commits to?

No — this is worth stating as plainly as the parallel questions modules 1 through 3 each raised
about their own crosswalks. A paper-based document-control process, properly controlled, is a
legitimate choice; nothing in AABB's framework or FDA regulation requires every site to run
document control electronically. The migration target in this module is Lakeshore's own
operational decision, made because an undated "pending migration" is weaker than a dated one, not
because any regulator demanded the system itself change.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Does the reconciled CMDB-and-catalog entry fully satisfy a security assessor running an ISO 27001 or SOC 2-style review of the eQMS?

Not fully, and the honest answer matters more than a confident one. The artifact gives strong
evidence toward the one domain that already cleanly matches the eQMS's RMF-selected controls
(access control, via account and identity management), but `itil-to-grc-crosswalk` already found
two domains — supplier relationships and business continuity — with no counterpart at all in the
eQMS's existing control set. Nothing built in this module closes those two domains, because
Lakeshore's RMF selection was never asked to cover them. The artifact is strong partial evidence
for a security assessor, not a complete answer.
:::

## Where this goes next

This module closed both gaps this course had been carrying since module 2 — a blank CMDB field,
now pointed at the RMF file that already answers it, and a reconciled service catalog with a
dated, owned path to closing its last real mismatch — and tested the result against three
different reviewers, honestly naming the one place it still falls short. The next module takes a
single underlying fact about the eQMS and shows how to present it two different ways, in CIO
language and in exec-quality-council language, without changing what it actually means.
